transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The Army says all of the degraded lead azide that sat nearly 20 years at an Iowa plant
is destroyed.
The military carried out a controlled detonation of the bomb-making material near Middletown
this morning to prevent thousands of pounds of the unstable material from accidentally
exploding.
Up until an hour before the blast, residents closest to the site were advised to evacuate
to avoid breathing toxic dust particles, but once it got closer to detonation time, FEMA
said it was too dangerous to evacuate until residents within a 20-mile radius to stay
indoors.
As residents prepare to celebrate Thanksgiving tomorrow, they're also waiting to learn if
the soil, air, or water has been contaminated.
EPA teams will conduct testing near the plant and outlying areas.
The stock market ended mixed today after some big swings earlier, and PR Scott Horsley
reports investors got both good and bad news from the Commerce Department.
A fresh, gross domestic product report from the Commerce Department says the U.S. economy
grew even faster than initially thought in July, August, and September.
GDP grew at an annual rate of 4.3 percent in the third quarter.
That's the strongest showing in three years, fueled by robust consumer spending and the
massive investment in artificial intelligence.
Faster growth comes with an unwelcome side effect, however.
Higher inflation prices in October were up 3.8 percent from a year ago, according to
the Commerce Department's inflation gauge, which is closely tracked by the Federal Reserve.
The Fed is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate next month in an effort to bring
prices under control.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
In Southern California, flood advisories remain in effect for a large swath of the coastline.
Until after Thanksgiving, NPR's Kirk Sigler reports, many coastal communities hit hard
in recent months have scrambled to prepare for this so-called "king tide" event.
A now common sound of equipment dredging harbors and dozers pushing sand onto beaches as the
powerful El Nino has warmed the Pacific Ocean, creating huge waves and sea levels a foot
higher than normal.
Steps from the water in Huntington Beach, Cat Reeves, has sandbags four feet high around
his apartment.
"Only because this is the new times, this is what you gotta do."
Reeves canceled his plans to fly to Texas to see his daughter for Thanksgiving as he
was worried about his place.
"It's never the end of the world, you know.
It's just something you gotta deal with and stuff, but I love it here."
Presidents here say this week's king tide could be a test for even larger swells predicted
by Christmas.
Kirk Sigler, NPR News, Huntington Beach, California.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 164 points and the day at 50,182.
The NASDAQ was down 147 points, roughly half a percent.
This is NPR News.
Storm-related wind could derail the 100th annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade tomorrow.
We have yet to formally hear if the show goes on as planned Thanksgiving Day or is delayed.
The event typically draws millions of spectators year after year, especially for a front row
seat to the parade's iconic giant balloons.
American utility customers are not alone.
In grappling with high energy prices in Britain, energy bills are expected to soar by 26% starting
in January.
Here's NPR's Lauren Freire.
The vast majority of British homes are heated with natural gas, making this country especially
vulnerable to price spikes caused by the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament his government is sending millions of British
households a one-time payment of 100 pounds, about $130, to help cover winter heating costs.
"The support we have provided alongside the removal of VAT from electricity bills will
give people some breathing space, but I accept there is more to do."
Wholesale gas prices are up about 33% over the past three months and have more than doubled
since this time last year.
Many Brits say they'll turn down or even off their heat this winter and layer up indoors
instead.
Lauren Freire, NPR News, London.
San Sebastian, Puerto Rico is celebrating a regal victory for one of its own.
The moment, Jennifer Barreto, was crowned Miss Universe to last night's pageant in San
Juan, Puerto Rico, as heard via the Associated Press.
Barreto made history as the first married woman and first mother to win Miss Universe.
I'm Lakshmi Singh, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Army completes controlled detonation of degraded lead azide at Iowa plant near Middletown
U.S. third-quarter GDP grows 4.3 percent, fastest in three years, as October inflation rises to 3.8 percent
Southern California flood advisories and king tide preparations ahead of larger swells by Christmas
Dow closes up 164 points at 50,182 while NASDAQ falls about half a percent
Storm winds threaten Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, delay not yet announced
British energy bills to rise 26 percent in January; Prime Minister Burnham announces 100-pound heating payment
Jennifer Barreto of Puerto Rico crowned Miss Universe, first married woman and mother to win
